lessons.title: Managed AD resilience: surviving a domain-controller or Availability Zone failure
lessons.layout: failure scenario with separate live resilience and backup recovery responsibilities
lessons.body:
Header "AWS SECURITY • DIRECTORY RESILIENCE", exact top-right sequence "29". Title "MANAGED AD: KEEP AUTHENTICATION REACHABLE". Premise "Two domain controllers across Availability Zones provide directory resilience; application availability is a separate design." Teach a concrete failure scenario, not another directory-choice overview. Draw a clear AWS VPC with TWO separate AZ boundaries. AZ 1 contains one AWS Managed AD domain controller labelled "DC 1 • unavailable" in dim blue with a red small failure indicator. AZ 2 contains one domain controller "DC 2 • available" in teal/green. Both belong to one "AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory"; no single controller between the AZs. Outside both AZ boxes but within VPC put a surviving client/workload with two labelled paths: failed path to DC 1, healthy path to DC 2 "DNS + directory authentication". Explicit annotation "Clients need working DNS, discovery and network paths to the surviving controller." Do not promise every app automatically fails over without configuration.
Below main diagram, a compact responsibility split with meaningful dimensional objects: "AWS manages directory hosts, replication and failed-controller replacement"; "You configure clients, networking and application resilience." A separate backup/recovery inset illustrates snapshot archive → directory restoration with wording "Backups support recovery; they are not the live failover path." Include a small worked validation checklist "Test new sign-in • Resolve directory DNS • Verify application access". No standby app platform or recreated app in failed AZ. Gentle glossy sapphire and teal directory objects, quiet navy behind sharp text, coral only for the failed DC; subtle orange for validation. No thick glowing frames, fake AWS logos, repeated podium grid or tiny body copy.

lessons.title: AD Connector troubleshooting: restore the directory path before changing IAM
lessons.layout: WAN failure evidence and targeted directory-path retest
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • DIRECTORY TROUBLESHOOTING", top-right "30". Title "AD CONNECTOR: THE DIRECTORY PATH MATTERS". Premise "AD Connector proxies directory requests; it does not keep a local directory replica for a WAN outage." Show a supported AWS application's new sign-in request → AD Connector gateway inside AWS VPC → VPN / Direct Connect link → separate on-premises AD domain controllers. Put a visible broken-link marker in the WAN connection, not at the gateway. Label the observed outcome "New directory authentication fails". A compact evidence note "Connector reachable • on-premises directory path unavailable". Explain clearly "Existing sessions or cached application state may behave differently." Do not imply every active user is instantly logged out. Lower diagnostic path on open navy: "Check hybrid routing" → "Test DNS and required AD traffic" → "Confirm domain-controller health" → "Retry a new sign-in". Supporting words "Review firewall and security-group paths" and "Confirm name resolution, time and directory reachability". No unsupported exhaustive port list, fake logs or runnable commands. A small standalone diagram contrasts a gateway icon with crossed-out replica document: "No directory-data caching or replication". Final useful note "Adding an S3 or IAM Allow does not restore an unavailable AD path." Use polished teal gateway, sapphire workload and violet on-premises servers; red only at failed WAN. Keep crisp readable labels, no repeated three-column grid or extra pedestals. This is a worked diagnostic, not a screenshot.

lessons.title: Trust direction follows the resource domain, while users travel the opposite way
lessons.layout: worked one-way trust and opposite user-access direction
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • DIRECTORY TRUST", top-right "31". Title "TRUST DIRECTION: FOLLOW THE RESOURCE". Premise "For users in Corp to access resources in AWS, the AWS resource domain trusts the Corp identity domain." Two clear domain zones ONLY: left "Corp domain • identities" with user group and domain controller; right "AWS Managed AD domain • resources" with a directory and EC2-hosted app. Across the top between domains, one orange arrow FROM RIGHT AWS domain TO LEFT Corp domain labeled "Trust: AWS trusts Corp". Next to RIGHT end label "Trusting domain • Outgoing"; next to LEFT end label "Trusted domain • Incoming". Across bottom a separate cyan arrow FROM LEFT Corp users TO RIGHT AWS resource labeled "Intended user access: Corp → AWS resources". Do not confuse these opposite directions or turn the access arrow into directory replication. Small worked test "Corp user signs in to permitted AWS-domain app" with note "Trust enables cross-domain authentication; resource authorization is still required." A small separate prerequisites checklist "VPN / Direct Connect • DNS forwarding • required AD traffic • matching trust type on both sides". Additional distinct note "Some AWS application integrations require a two-way trust; verify the application's requirement." Do not claim a one-way trust works for IAM Identity Center or every AWS managed app. Another small note "Trust does not copy user accounts between domains." High-contrast navy, subtle glossy violet identity objects, teal AWS resource objects, clean orange trust and cyan access arrows; avoid giant panels, tiny footnotes, fake logos or broad universal ALLOW.

lessons.title: A self-managed EC2 domain-controller replica can reduce WAN authentication dependence
lessons.layout: same-domain replication path and local authentication during WAN failure
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • HYBRID DIRECTORY DESIGN", top-right "32". Title "LOCAL DC REPLICA: A DIFFERENT RESPONSIBILITY". Premise "A self-managed domain controller on EC2 is a replica of the existing domain, not an AD Connector cache." Worked architecture: left corporate site contains "On-premises domain controller" and domain label "corp.example.com". Right AWS VPC contains "Self-managed DC on EC2" also labelled "corp.example.com" plus an application/client. A two-direction connection between the two domain controllers is labelled "AD replication over VPN / Direct Connect". Add a small red interruption symbol on this WAN path for the illustrated outage. Within AWS VPC, local app → local EC2 DC shows "Local DNS + authentication path". Explicit conditional outcome "Local authentication can continue subject to replication state and application design." Do not promise all workloads or access to on-premises resources keep working. Lower ownership note with EC2 administration objects "You operate DC patching, replication, backups and recovery." Separate trade-off note "Monitor replication health and stale identity changes after a WAN interruption." Contrast with a smaller AD Connector gateway below: "AD Connector alone has no local directory replica." No trust arrow between these two same-domain replica DCs, no claim replica automatically becomes separate AWS Managed Microsoft AD forest, no new IAM-user credentials, no absolute uptime guarantee. Use blue/violet matching-domain labels, polished service objects, understated green local path and orange replication connector. Varied layout, concise readable labels and moderate depth; no platform under every node.

lessons.title: Application SSO requires a separate application assignment and correct attribute mapping
lessons.layout: customer-managed SAML app configuration and browser-mediated sign-in
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • APPLICATION SINGLE SIGN-ON", top-right "33". Title "APP SSO: ASSIGN THE APP, MAP THE CLAIMS". Premise "An AWS account permission-set assignment does not automatically grant access to a business application." Make the main example explicitly "Customer-managed SAML application". Upper configuration story: IAM Identity Center application configuration links "Service-provider metadata + assertion consumer URL", "Required attribute mappings" and "Assigned users or groups" to a business-app object. Example attribute mapping in readable simple text "App Username ← Identity Center email" marked "Illustrative mapping; follow app requirements". Lower precise runtime browser sequence: employee browser opens assigned app from AWS access portal; IAM Identity Center issues app SAML response via the browser; browser POSTs response to "Application service provider"; application establishes its session after validating claims. Draw arrows to/from the browser correctly; no AWS STS credentials returned to business app and no permission-set-to-app access arrow. A side comparison note "AWS managed apps: configure integration and assignments in the relevant service console or API." Another note "The application still controls its own roles and data permissions." A worked failure example "Signed in, no app tile? Check direct group membership and app assignment." No nested-group support claim, universal auto-assignment, fake branded SaaS logos or exact console screenshot. Glossy violet IdentityCenter objects, teal browser, sapphire business app, orange mapping connectors. Do not impose a three-panel grid; let config and runtime sections be clearly separated without big frames.

lessons.title: Identity Center access-control mappings override matching SAML attribute values
lessons.layout: conflicting trusted attribute values resolve to one session tag
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • ATTRIBUTE MAPPING", exact top-right "34". Title "ONE TAG, TWO VALUES: WHICH SOURCE WINS?". Premise "For Identity Center access-control attributes, a configured directory mapping takes precedence over the matching SAML value." A precise worked evidence diagram with two inputs: upper source "Identity Center directory" shows "Department = Finance" and is connected through "Configured Attributes for access control mapping"; lower source "External IdP SAML assertion" shows "Department = HR". These two inputs feed a modest resolution mechanism, whose single output is "Role-session tag: Department = Finance". Clearly mark the directory-mapped path selected, the SAML HR value replaced for this matching attribute. Do not show two Department tags in the session or combine both permissions. A second smaller case below: "No mapping for this key?" → "A correctly configured SAML access-control attribute can supply the session tag." Explain "This precedence is for access-control attributes; application attribute mappings are a separate configuration." Verification path "Check source value → inspect mapping → obtain a fresh session → verify expected policy scope". Security note "Trust and protect the attribute source; users must not self-assign privileged values." Use a polished sapphire directory record, violet SAML document and teal selected session-tag object; exact label areas matte, moderate gloss on objects. No broad unconditional ALLOW or runnable policy code, no copy of the prior ABAC resource-matching slide's layout.

lessons.title: SAML assertion claims and role trust must agree before STS issues a session
lessons.layout: assertion evidence passes named identity and trust checks
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • SAML ASSERTION CHECKS", top-right "35". Title "SAML CLAIMS: MATCH THE ROLE AND THE REQUEST". Premise "A signed assertion must identify the intended role, provider and user session, and satisfy the role's trust." Label the worked path explicitly "Direct IAM SAML federation". Left a modest signed SAML assertion document with readable shorthand fields: "Role: role ARN + SAML provider ARN"; "RoleSessionName: alice_01"; "Recipient + time conditions". Add small explicit label "Claim names shown in shorthand". Center an STS validation/trust gate checks "Trusted provider + signature", "Required claims and intended endpoint", "Role trust conditions". Output right "Temporary role session" with three-credential key bundle, not application JWT. Lower concise evidence notes: "RoleSessionName cannot contain spaces." "Use exact, case-sensitive AWS attribute Name URIs." A separate trust-action evidence area, compact but readable: "Base operation: sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML"; "Passing session tags also needs sts:TagSession"; "Passing SourceIdentity also needs sts:SetSourceIdentity". Show these last two as conditional additions, not requirements for every SAML login. Failure evidence "Missing required claim or trust permission → no session" with note "Check the actual error before changing policies." No XML, no invented ARN strings, no claim that RoleSessionName determines permissions. Keep terms accurate, readable, use polished purple assertion, teal trust checks and blue credential object with minimal framing.

lessons.title: Direct SAML role-session lifetime follows allowed duration and assertion limits
lessons.layout: worked expiration timeline and over-limit request contrast
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • FEDERATED SESSION LIFETIME", exact top-right "36". Title "SAML SESSION: CHECK THE EARLIEST DEADLINE". Premise "In a direct AssumeRoleWithSAML API call, the issued role session can end before the requested duration." Main worked example explicitly "Illustrative times, direct API session": "Requested DurationSeconds: 2 hours"; "Role maximum: 4 hours"; "SAML SessionNotOnOrAfter: 1 hour from now". Show one clean horizontal elapsed-time timeline from "Now" through "+1h", "+2h", "+4h". A vivid teal actual credential lifetime ends AT +1h. Ghost outline requested duration ends at +2h; a distinct bracket marks role maximum+4h. Output "Session expires at +1h in this example". Make no rule that duration is always the role maximum or always the assertion's short NotOnOrAfter freshness value. Lower distinct contrasting request: "Request 6h with a 4h role maximum → request fails" (not silently shortened). Two short operational notes "Read Expiration in the STS response." and "Assertion validity and issued credential lifetime are distinct checks." Scope note "IAM Identity Center permission-set sessions and portal sessions use their own settings." Do not imply direct AssumeRoleWithSAML works on AWSReservedSSO_ roles or universal console behavior. Glossy clock, signed assertion and credential objects support the time mechanism without decorative oversize clocks. Cyan/violet/orange distinctions, crisp modest font, no tiny timestamps or huge cards.

lessons.title: Applied checkpoint: separate sign-in, account assignment and allowed actions
lessons.layout: one incident evidence trail with expected and missing authorization outcomes
lessons.body: Header "AWS SECURITY • APPLIED CHECKPOINT", exact top-right "37". Title "SIGNED IN IS NOT THE SAME AS AUTHORIZED". Premise "Trace the identity, assignment and requested action before deciding whether access is broken or correctly restricted." One coherent incident story with illustrative evidence, NOT three unrelated question cards. Employee portal on left shows "Sign-in: successful" and "Group: OpsReaders". Central assignment ledger as a compact two-row example: "Development account | OpsReaders | ReadOnly | assigned"; "Production account | OpsReaders | ReadOnly | not assigned". Make it a clear evidence ledger, not a fake exact AWS console. A callout asks "Why is Production missing from the portal?" then diagnosis "No Production assignment for this group." Below, an authorized change path "If approved: add the intended scoped assignment → refresh and retest account visibility". Do not suggest granting access without approval or assigning AdministratorAccess. A second observation AFTER that correct assignment is shown as the next stage of the same incident: "Production ReadOnly session: ec2:StartInstances denied". Decision explanation "This can be the intended result of read-only access, not an authentication failure." Conclude with useful retest checks "Confirm correct account and role • Test an allowed read action • Keep unapproved write actions restricted". Use modest polished browser, group, assignment document and role-session objects; teal for proven identity, amber for missing assignment, violet for restricted write. Clear event order, no arbitrary privileges, no giant decorative security shield or quiz widgets. Preserve teaching depth with readable concise copy.
